review.independentMath: A champion with k games has a final opponent with at least k-2 games. Disjoint participant sets give M0=1, M1=2, Mk=M(k-1)+M(k-2). This bound is achieved by combining those two minimum tournaments and choosing the k-1-game player to win. A 1-game champion can represent any n>=2 by repeatedly letting a newcomer beat the existing 1-game champion; inductively a k-game champion can represent any n>=Mk. Thus max{k:Mk<=n} is exactly the answer, including the largest valid n=10^18 (answer 85).

legalLfWitness.constraints: Single test case, one nonempty line containing one decimal integer n; 2 <= n <= 1000000000000000000

proof.implementedAlgorithm: Read x; bit-test whether x is a power of two using x&(x-1). For powers of two print int(log2(x)); otherwise print floor(log2(x))+1. This counts balanced binary-bracket depth, not the maximal games allowed by the difference-of-games rule.

independentMathematicalCertificate.lowerBoundProof: Let M(k) be the minimum number of players for a champion with k games. M(0)=1, M(1)=2. Before its kth win the champion has k-1 games; its final opponent must have at least k-2 games by the permitted difference <=1. Their elimination subtrees are disjoint. Induction gives M(k)>=M(k-1)+M(k-2). Conversely join minimum subtrees with k-1 and k-2 games, let the former win, and the bound is attained. Thus M(k)=M(k-1)+M(k-2).
independentMathematicalCertificate.upperBoundProof: The included finite construction DAG covers ALL n players, not just M(k) of them. Each node expands to two DISJOINT fresh copies of its child templates, and its listed left winner wins their final match. Leaf=one player, no games. All child player counts sum to the parent, and every listed final match has pre-match game-count difference <=1. Expanded tournament has n-1 matches and the listed root champion games. Identical child templates are copied, not shared players.
